references.text: Jesus' commissioning speech in Matthew contains the same instruction to shake the dust off one's feet when leaving a city or house that does not receive the disciples, with the addition that it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment.
Mark's parallel account of the sending out of the twelve, where Jesus gives the same command to shake the dust off one's feet as a testimony against those who do not receive the disciples.

In the sending out of the seventy(-two), Jesus gives similar instructions to go into the streets of a city that does not receive them and say that the dust clinging to their feet should be wiped off as a testimony against them.
Paul and Barnabas shook the dust off their feet against the inhabitants of Antioch in Pisidia when they were driven out, as a practical fulfillment of Jesus' command in the commissioning speech.

Paul shook the dust from his clothes and said, 'Your blood be on your own heads,' when the Jews in Corinth opposed him – a similar symbolic act serving as testimony against those who rejected the message.
Nehemiah shook out the folds of his robe as a symbolic gesture and curse, which shows the Old Testament background for the symbolic act of shaking off dust as a testimony.

Ezekiel is told to warn the wicked, and if the wicked do not turn from their ways, they will die for their sin, but Ezekiel has saved his life – this principle of testifying and then freeing oneself from responsibility underlies Jesus' words about shaking off the dust as a testimony.
